summary: Warns that protocols such as ARP and Neighbor Discovery carry link-layer addresses whose bit order differs between LAN technologies. Implementors must take care to use the canonical form so that all parties interpret the bits the same way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some places write dates month first and others write the day first, so a date can be misread. Some networks write address bits in a different order in the same way.

subtitle: A warning that LAN adapters disagree on the bit order of addresses, so protocols like ARP and Neighbor Discovery can break.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as ARP and Neighbor Discovery carry link-layer addresses in data fields, but Token Ring and some FDDI hardware map the bits of an address into memory in a different order from Ethernet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines canonical form (the Ethernet format), shows how it differs from the MSB format with an example address, and tells implementors to bit-swap individual bytes when an adapter is not canonical.
tldr.outcome: Fields that require canonical form must carry canonical addresses. Bridges between Token Ring and Ethernet bit-swap the addresses inside forwarded ARP packets.

facts.label: Canonical form
facts.value: Also called LSB or Ethernet format

facts.label: Non-canonical form
facts.value: Also called MSB, IBM or Token-Ring format

today: RFC 2469 is an Informational memo from December 1998, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It is advice for implementors, not a standard.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
Protocols such as ARP and Neighbor Discovery have data fields that hold link-layer addresses. For two machines to interoperate, the sender must make sure the receiver extracts those bits and interprets them correctly. In most cases the field must be in canonical form.

Not all LAN adapters are consistent in their use of canonical form, so an implementation may need to bit swap individual bytes to get the right format.
sections.plainLanguage: If two people read the same number but one starts from the left and one from the right, they get different answers. Computers can make the same mistake with addresses.

sections.title: Canonical and Non-Canonical Form
sections.content:
Canonical form, also called "LSB format" or "Ethernet format", is defined by how bits on the LAN map to bits in memory: the first bit of each byte that appears on the LAN maps to the least significant (right-most) bit of the byte in memory. This puts the group address indicator, the bit that says unicast or multicast, in the least significant bit of the first byte. Ethernet and 802.3 hardware behave this way.

Token Ring and some FDDI hardware map the first bit of each byte to the most significant bit instead. This is called "MSB format", "IBM format", "Token-Ring format" or non-canonical form, and it puts the group address indicator in the most significant bit of the first byte.

For the canonical address 12-34-56-78-9A-BC, the MSB-format bytes in memory are 48 2C 6A 1E 59 3D. Addresses taken from or given to adapters, or read from link-layer headers, may need bit-swapping to reach canonical form.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine writing each byte of the address backwards. Ethernet writes it one way, Token Ring the other way.

sections.title: Trouble Spots in IPv6 and IPv4
sections.content:
All the IPv6-over-link-layer documents require link-layer addresses to be sent in canonical order. The authors say all Ethernet adapters use canonical order, so no special processing is needed there, while some FDDI and all Token Ring adapters appear to use non-canonical format. Implementors must send addresses in Neighbor Discovery link-layer address options in canonical order and interpret received ones correctly.

For ARP, Ethernet addresses are in canonical order, but over Token Ring the de facto practice is non-canonical order. On one Token Ring this causes no problem, since every adapter assumes non-canonical order. Across a Token Ring and Ethernet bridge, communication would fail, so bridges between dissimilar network types bit-swap the addresses in the address fields of forwarded ARP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator standing between two groups fixes the backwards addresses so both sides understand each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that there are no known security issues raised by this document. It is informational, aimed at helping implementors avoid using non-canonical forms where canonical ones are required.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say they know of no safety problems here, just a way to avoid mix-ups.
